Q_EC.text: I brought it up with my manager fairly early on, actually -- it was maybe three months into the job, and I'd been having some rough patches with anxiety that were making it hard to concentrate during certain kinds of meetings (particularly the ones with a lot of cross-talk and interruptions, which I find really dysregulating), and I just decided that being upfront was going to work better for me than trying to white-knuckle through it. my manager was genuinely receptive, which I know isn't everyone's experience, and we ended up having a pretty long conversation about what specific situations were hardest and what would actually help. What came out of it was a few concrete things -- I can now skip the larger all-hands meetings and catch the recording instead, and I have standing permission to work from home on days when I know it's going to be a high-anxiety period, and honestly just having that flexibility has made an enormous difference to how I function at work. I think the fact that I came in with specific asks rather than just a general disclosure helped a lot, because it gave my manager something actionable to respond to rather than putting them in awkward position of not knowing what to do, which in my experience is where a lot of those conversations break down even when the manager genuinely wants to help.

Q_CC.text: it's been mostly positive, honestly -- I've told a few close colleagues, not the whole team or anything, more the people I work with day-to-day and have built up some trust with. one of them actually has their own anxiety stuff going on so that conversation felt very natural, kind of a mutual disclosure that I think made us both feel less like we were managing something in secret. the others were a bit more uncertain at first, like you could tell they weren't quite sure what to say or whether to treat it as a big deal, but I think that's just people not having much practice with these conversations rather than any actual discomfort with me. what I've noticed is that once you normalise it a little -- just refer to it matter-of-factly rather than making it a heavy moment -- people tend to follow your lead, and now it's just sort of background knowledge that occasionally comes up when I need to explain why I'm dialling in instead of being in the room. nobody has ever been unkind about it and a couple of people have since mentioned their own mental health things to me, which I take as a sign that it shifted something small but real about what feels okay to talk about on our team, and that feels worth more to me than any individual conversation.

Q_CW.text: the one that stands out most is the colleague I mentioned having their own anxiety -- what happened was we were debriefing after a particularly chaotic sprint review, the kind where everything ran over and there were a lot of competing voices, and I had said something offhand about finding that kind of meeting hard to manage, and they just kind of paused and said "yeah, me too, actually, more than people probably realise." and then it turned into a proper conversation, maybe twenty minutes, where they talked about how they'd been managing it mostly by just quietly leaving situations before they got bad and hoping no one noticed, which I thought was pretty revealing because it showed how much energy people spend just on concealment rather than actually coping. they hadn't told anyone at work before, and I think the reason they told me was that I had already made it seem like a normal thing to talk about rather than a confession. I tried to share some of what had worked for me in terms of talking to management, and I think they found that useful, though I don't know whether they ever followed through on it -- it's their call to make and I didn't want to push. but honestly that conversation is part of why I think being open matters beyond just your own situation, because it creates a kind of permission structure for other people who are carrying the same things in silence

Q_PE.text: the previous role was a bit more mixed, honestly -- I did disclose there too, because by that point I'd already worked out that trying to hide it just costs too much in terms of energy and pretending, but the reaction was more of a sort of polite acknowledgment without a lot of follow-through. my manager at the time said the right things in the moment, something like "of course, we want to support you," but when it came to actually changing anything practical it kind of just... didn't happen, there was always something more urgent and I think they genuinely didn't know what accommodations would even look like. I don't think there was any ill will, more just a lack of framework for what to actually do, which is probably pretty common, and I think that experience is actually a big part of why I came into the conversation with my current manager with specific asks already prepared rather than leaving it open-ended -- I'd learned that a vague disclosure without a concrete request doesn't really give anyone anything to act on.

Q_PC.text: at that previous job the coworker conversations were a bit more mixed than they've been in my current role -- I told maybe two or three people, again not widely, and the reactions were kind of what you'd expect from a workplace that didn't have a lot of existing culture around talking about this stuff openly. one person was very warm and immediately shared that they'd had their own experiences with depression, which surprised me a bit because they were quite senior and I hadn't expected that kind of reciprocity, and that was a genuinely good conversation. the others were more the kind of well-meaning-but-awkward response where you can tell someone is trying to say the right thing but doesn't quite have the vocabulary for it (a lot of "I'm sure it'll get better" type responses, which are kind -- I don't want to be uncharitable about it -- but don't really engage with what you've said). I don't think anyone was unkind or that it affected how they worked with me in any negative way, but it also didn't shift anything about the team culture the way I feel like it has in my current job, which I think is partly about the individuals and partly about whether the broader environment makes it feel safe to take that step. I came away from that job thinking that individual openness can only do so much if the organisation itself hasn't created the conditions for it to land well, which is something I feel pretty strongly about now in terms of what makes workplaces actually supportive rather than just not actively hostile

Q_CA.text: honestly, less than I feared it would, and I think that's partly luck in terms of where I've ended up and partly about how you frame it. I've never been passed over for anything that I know of, and if anything I think being matter-of-fact about it has made me come across as more self-aware rather than less competent -- which isn't the narrative you usually hear but has genuinely been my experience. the one thing I do think about is that I can't be completely certain what I don't know, like there could be conversations happening that I'm not privy to, but I've decided that living in that uncertainty and staying silent costs more than any risk that comes from being open, so I just try not to dwell on the hypotheticals too much.

Q_BH.text: I think the clearest example is what I described with the previous employer -- I had the conversation, it felt okay in the room, my manager said all the supportive things, and then nothing changed. no follow-up meeting, no specific adjustments, just a kind of vague goodwill that didn't translate into anything practical. the thing that made it feel badly handled in retrospect wasn't hostility, it was more the slow realisation that the conversation had essentially been absorbed and nothing had shifted, and I was still white-knuckling through the same situations that had prompted me to say something in the first place (the high-interruption meetings, the unpredictable schedule changes, all of it). I don't think it was malicious at all but I do think it was a failure of knowing what to actually do with a disclosure, and tbh that experience taught me more about how to have these conversations effectively than any of the good ones have -- like, I learned that you can't just disclose and hope, you have to come in with specific asks.

Q_SH.text: the clearest example is the one I've already touched on with my current manager, but what made it genuinely well-handled wasn't just the initial conversation -- it was what happened after, which is where I think most supportive intentions fall apart. my manager actually followed up maybe two weeks later, not in a formal way, just a quick check-in to ask whether the changes we'd discussed were actually helping or whether we needed to adjust anything, and that follow-up mattered more to me than almost anything else because it signalled that the conversation hadn't just been filed away somewhere and forgotten. it meant I wasn't carrying the burden of having to re-raise it if something wasn't working, which is a huge thing psychologically because re-disclosing always costs something even when you know the environment is safe. I think what made it work was a combination of my manager being comfortable sitting with the specifics rather than rushing to reassure me in generic terms, and honestly the fact that our workplace has some existing culture around flexibility that meant my asks didn't feel like I was requesting something outlandish -- the infrastructure was already there in a way, I just needed someone to apply it to my situation explicitly rather than assuming I'd navigate it myself.

Q_ID.text: the biggest thing, I think, is moving away from the model where mental health support is something reactive that only gets activated when someone is already in crisis -- because by that point you've already lost most of the value, both for the person and for the organisation. what actually works, in my experience, is when accommodation is built into the culture before anyone needs to ask for it: flexible working as a default rather than a negotiated exception, meeting structures that don't assume everyone processes information the same way, managers who've actually been trained to have these conversations rather than just having good intentions and no framework. the stigma piece is related but I think it's worth separating out -- a lot of employers seem to think "mental health support" means having an EAP hotline listed somewhere on the intranet, when actually the most stigma-reducing thing you can do is have leaders talk openly about their own experiences, because that changes what feels sayable across the whole organisation in a way that a wellness app or a leaflet never will. and honestly I think the tech industry specifically has an advantage here because it tends to attract people who respond well to explicit norms, so if you make "we talk about this openly here" part of actual onboarding culture rather than just aspirational language in a values document, it tends to stick -- the infrastructure for normalising it is already kind of there, its just a question of whether anyone decides to actually use it

Q_EC.text: Was having a particularly bad anxiety episode that had lasted a few days and was negatively affecting work so I asked if I could take a few days off, and explained why. He said yes, and we now have open communication about my illness and he allows me some "exceptions" from rules. Such as I have more flexible work hours, and I can work from home when I need to. I can take "anxiety days" when I need to. I do take them unpaid since that gives me less anxiety and then it doesn't show on the budget higher up (A large company has a small office in my country and these are all arrangements at that office.) but he is fine with me taking them as paid sick days, again my choice not to do so. All I have to do is inform my team when I'm showing up very late or not at all or working from home, it is such a relief to be able to have honest open communication and has lessened a lot of anxiety that I had about "being sick a lot" or if they thought I was a lazy person. My anxiety also affects my sleep a lot and now since making these adjustments I have not had to show up for work unslept and the even though I have fewer hours some weeks then I did before they are more productive and I'm happier about them. He did ask a lot about if there was anything at work that was making things worse and what they could do better, and when they were changing up teams at my office I was asked before anything was finalized.

Q_EC.text: I spoke with both my manager and HR when PTSD symptoms from a prior workplace incident started affecting my concentration and my ability to be in certain spaces. HR was genuinely helpful -- they arranged EAP sessions and gave me some flexibility around where I could work. My manager was a bit awkward at first, honestly I think the specifics caught them off guard, but they came around and checked in regularly after that.

Q_CC.text: A couple of close colleagues knew what had happened -- not the full picture, but enough that they understood why I was sometimes avoiding certain areas of the office. One of them had dealt with anxiety herself so she got it pretty quickly, no real explanation needed. The other was more uncertain about how to react I think, but they were kind about it and mostly just carried on normally which was actually what I needed.

Q_CW.text: She brought it up quietly one afternoon, said she'd been dealing with anxiety for a few years and wanted me to know in case she ever seemed off or needed to step away from something. Honestly it felt like an act of trust more than anything -- she wasn't asking for anything specific, just wanted someone to know. I told her I appreciated her telling me and mentioned I had my own stuff going on, which is how we ended up being pretty open with each other. No big moment, just a quiet conversation that made the working relationship easier.

Q_PE.text: That employer was actually the source of the problem, so it's a different kind of conversation. I did raise concerns -- not framed as mental health at the time, more about the situation itself and feeling unsafe. It wasn't taken seriously. HR was dismissive and my manager at the time was part of what I was trying to report, so there wasn't really a neutral party to go to. Nothing was addressed. That experience is a big part of why I'm more deliberate now about reading workplace culture before disclosing anything.

Q_PC.text: I was pretty guarded in that environment -- when you're not sure who's safe and the problem is coming from above, you don't really know which coworkers might loop back to management. There was one person I trusted enough to say something to, and she was sympathetic, but honestly she was also trying to keep her own head down. I dont think either of us felt like there was much we could do. Most of my other colleagues had no idea what was going on.

Q_CA.text:
It's mixed, honestly. In my previous role the disclosure -- or really, just raising concerns at all -- contributed to me leaving a situation that was already untenable. That set me back professionally and I spent a while being very careful about what I said and to whom.

In my current context it's been different. I gave a talk on anxiety at a company event and it was well received, and if anything it's opened some doors -- conversations about wellbeing initiatives, being seen as someone who can speak to this stuff. I don't think it's hurt my standing. But I'm also aware that not every workplace would have reacted the same way, and I made deliberate choices about where to work partly based on that.

Q_BH.text: The situation at my previous workplace involved targeted behavior from a manager that made me genuinely fear for my safety at times. When I raised this with HR -- carefully, because I knew I was in a vulnerable position -- the response was to question whether I was interpreting things correctly. there was a suggestion I was being oversensitive. My manager was actually present in one of those early conversations, which made the whole thing collapse before it really started. Nothing was documented, nothing followed up, and I eventually left because staying felt untenable.

Q_SH.text: When I disclosed to HR at my current employer, the contrast with what I'd experienced before was pretty stark. I gave them enough context to explain what I needed without laying out the full history, and they took it at face value -- no pushback, no suggestion I was misreading things. They connected me with the EAP quickly and worked out a practical arrangement around workspace flexibility without making it a whole process. My manager needed a little time to find their footing, but they asked what would actually help rather than assuming, which made a real difference. I think what made it work was that the people involved treated it as a practical problem to solve rather than something to manage me around.

Q_ID.text: The biggest gap I've seen is managers not knowing what to do with a disclosure once it happens -- training tends to stop at "be supportive" without giving people concrete next steps. Beyond that, I think neutral reporting channels matter more than most companies admit, because if the problem involves someone's direct manager the whole structure falls apart. And honestly, just normalizing the conversation earlier would help. Not waiting for a crisis to be the first time mental health comes up.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer situation, essentially. I flagged that I was struggling to stay organized and asked about flexibility in deadlines -- the response was a meeting with my manager where the takeaway was that I needed better time management strategies. No follow-up, no HR involvement. It was framed kindly enough that I second-guessed whether I'd even asked clearly.

Q_SH.text: My current employer, when I disclosed the bipolar diagnosis and asked for leave. My manager listened without visibly minimizing it, said the right things about it being a health issue like any other, and escalated to HR without making me feel like I was creating a problem. The accommodations -- flexible return timeline, adjusted deadlines -- were formalized in writing. It was handled the way it should be, which I only fully appreciated by contrast with my previous experience.

Q_ID.text: Normalize disclosure before a crisis forces it. Formal accommodations matter, but honestly the informal culture -- whether managers treat it as a legitimate health issue or a performance problem -- is what determines whether people feel safe asking in the first place.

Q_AE.text: Peer support networks -- informal ones that exist between colleagues who've disclosed to each other -- probably do more day-to-day than any formal policy. Worth studying, if that's useful.

Q_EC.text: i told my manager i was dealing with major depression and recovering from alcoholism -- felt like the right thing, being upfront. big mistake. he used it in a performance review maybe two months later, framing me as unreliable, said my "judgment had been affected." no support was offered, no EAP mention, nothing. just a quiet shift in how he talked about me to the rest of the team after that.

Q_CC.text: totally different experience than with my manager. a couple of coworkers already knew i was in recovery -- i'd told them during a rough stretch and they just... showed up. one guy in particular checked in on me regularly, brought me coffee when i was clearly struggling, never made it weird. it felt like actual friendship, not pity. that honestly kept me going more than anything the company ever did.

Q_CW.text: one of the same coworkers who'd supported me through my worst stretch came to me about a year in, said he'd been struggling with anxiety bad enough he wasn't sleeping. i think he felt safe because of what i'd shared. we ended up talking for like two hours -- it wasn't a big formal thing, just two people being honest. i was really glad he trusted me with it.

Q_PE.text: same situation, different job. i was more guarded that time around -- didn't get into specifics, just mentioned i was going through something personal and might need some flexibility. my manager nodded, said "of course," and then nothing changed. no follow-up, no resources mentioned. not hostile like the next job would be, just... indifferent.

Q_PC.text: didn't really open up to coworkers at that job -- i was keeping things pretty contained there. one person i was friendly with noticed i seemed off and asked if i was okay, i just said "going through some stuff" and she left it at that. no pressure, which i appreciated. but i wasn't close enough to anyone there to let them in the way i eventually did later.

Q_CA.text: directly, yeah. that performance review where my manager weaponized my disclosure -- i didn't get the promotion i was up for that cycle. i'm pretty sure that wasn't a coincidence. and there's this low-grade thing that follows you, where you wonder if every weird interaction or being left off a project is connected. it's hard to prove but hard to ignore too.

Q_BH.text: the review came out of nowhere -- i'd told him maybe eight weeks before, and things seemed fine on the surface. no warning signs. then i'm sitting across from him and he's reading from notes about "concerning judgment patterns" and "reliability concerns." i realized partway through that every example he cited mapped to the period i'd disclosed. he never said the word depression but it was obvious what he was doing.

Q_AE.text: just that the peer support piece genuinely saved me in a way no company policy ever has. i hope researchers actually look at that side of it, not just the bad management stories.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been more positive than I expected -- at least where I am now. Being open about it has actually built trust with people I work closely with, and I think it's made me a better collaborator. I'm not naive though; I've been selective about where and when I've disclosed, and I think that's part of why it hasn't cost me. Earlier in my career I kept it much closer to the chest, partly because I didn't know how it would land. That instinct wasn't wrong for that environment.

Q_SH.text: The conversation with my current manager when the anxiety peaked -- that one stands out. Q_ID.text: Stop treating mental health support as a liability management exercise -- that's the core thing. What actually works is managers who are trained to just LISTEN before they redirect, and cultures where disclosure doesn't feel like a career calculation. The industry tends to confuse policy with culture, and they're not the same thing at all.
